sentences.text: The State has preferred this appeal against judgment of acquittal passed by the Prl.District and Sessions Judge, Chamarajanagar in S.C. No.71/2012 dated 17.07.2015.
2. Parties are referred to as per their ranking before the trial Court, for the sake of convenience.

3. The brief facts of the prosecution case are that, the accused is the husband of Mangalamma having married her 15 years prior to the filing of the case, three children were born out of their wedlock.

It is the case of the prosecution that, the accused was subjecting Mangalamma to cruelty,
both physical and mental torture, harassing the deceased saying that she would not live.

It is stated that, on 25.05.2012 the accused while going to coolie work, picked up quarrel and abused NC:
2023:KHC:45293 her, at that time, he poured kerosene on her body and set fire.

4. On hearing cry of the victim, the neighbours admitted Mangalamma to Government Hospital,
Gundlupet.
PWs. 1 and 3 - the parents of Mangalamma visited the hospital after receipt of information.
The statement of the victim was recorded in the presence of Panchas and marked it as Ex.P5.
On the basis of statement, accused was arrested in Crime no.56/12 of Therekanambi Police station, Gundlupet.
After investigation, the IO submitted the charge sheet against the accused under Sections 498(A) and 306 of Indian Penal Code (for short 'IPC').
5. After filing of the charge sheet, the case was registered in CC No.393/2012 by the committal Court.
Thereafter, case was committed to the Court of Sessions and accused was arrested on 26.05.2012.
An application NC: 2023:KHC:45293 was filed to release the accused on bail.
On considering the application, the accused was enlarged on bail.

6. On hearing the parties, the Trial Court has framed the charges, read over and explained to the accused for the offences punishable under Sections 498A, 306 of IPC, the accused having understood, pleaded not guilty and claimed to be tried.
7. To prove the guilt of the accused, prosecution has examined in all 14 witnesses as PWs.1 to 14 and 12 documents were marked i.e. Exs. P1 to P12.
Four material objects were marked as MO Nos.1 to 4.
On closure of prosecution side evidence, 313 statement was recorded as to the incriminating circumstances found against the accused.
8. The accused totally denied the evidence of prosecution witnesses.
However accused has not adduced defence evidence on his behalf.
During the NC: 2023:KHC:45293 course of examination of Doctor PW.8 Dr.M.Jagadeesh, MLC
Extract copy is marked as Ex.D1.

11. Learned HCGP Sri M.R.Patil, submits his arguments that, the judgment and order of acquittal passed by the trial Court is contrary to the evidence on record and same is required to be set aside.
The trial Court has not properly appreciated the oral and documentary evidence in the proper perspective.
Same has resulted in miscarriage of justice.
12. PWs. 1 and 2 are the parents of deceased Mangalamma have spoken regarding the injuries sustained by the deceased.
In this regard it is stated that she was complaining to her parents that accused was NC: 2023:KHC:45293 harassing the victim.

The evidence of PWs. 1 and 2 discloses that the accused was subjecting the deceased both physically and mentally and it further establishes the act of accused having poured kerosene on the deceased and set fire.
13. The evidence of PWs.1 and 2 coupled with Ex.P1- Inquest Panchanama clearly establishes the guilt of the accused beyond reasonable doubt.
It can safely come to the conclusion that physical and mental cruelty and harassment by the accused to the deceased is proved.
The trial Court completely ignored the material evidence on record and also failed to appreciating the same which has resulted in miscarriage of justice.
14. Ex.P5 is the statement of the deceased recorded by PW.13 at Gundlupet Government Hospital where the injured was given treatment on 25.05.2012 between 11.30 p.m. and 12.00 hrs.
PW.8 - Dr.M.Jagadeesh was on duty has clearly deposed that NC: 2023:KHC:45293 deceased was in a fit condition to give statement regarding her injuries due to pouring of kerosene and setting fire.
On overall appreciation of the facts and circumstances clearly leads to a conclusion that deceased committed suicide on account of cruelty so meted out to her by the accused.
On all these grounds sought to allow this appeal.

15. As against this, the learned counsel appearing on behalf of respondent-accused submitted his argument that the trial Court has properly appreciated the evidence on record and law on the point and facts.

The MLC register Extract vide Ex.D1 reveals that the Mangalamma was admitted to the hospital in view of accidental burn injuries due to burst of kerosene pump stove when she was trying to lit the stove at her house at about 7.30 p.m. on 25.5.2012 and her husband I.e. accused also sustained injuries all over the body.

The trial Court has assigned the proper reasons and passed the impugned judgment of acquittal that there are no grounds to interfere with the impugned judgment of acquittal.

18. Before adverting to the actual facts of the case and appreciation of evidence, it is necessary to refer the dictum of Hon'ble Supreme Court with regard to scope and power of Appellate Court in appeal against the order of acquittal.

19. In the case of MOTIRAM PADU JOSHI & OTHERS v. STATE OF MAHARASHTRA1 at paragraph 23 of the judgment, it is held thus:
"23.

While considering the scope of power of the appellate court in an appeal against the order of acquittal, after referring to various judgments, in Chandrappa v. State of Karnataka, (2007)4 SCC 415, this Court summarised the principle as under:-
"42.

entities.text: Chandrappa v. State of Karnataka, (2007)4 SCC 415
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
From the above decisions, in our considered view, the following general principles regarding powers of the appellate court while dealing with an appeal against an order of acquittal emerge:
(1) An appellate court has full power to review, re-appreciate and 2018 SCC OnLine SC 676 - 10 - NC: 2023:KHC:45293 reconsider the evidence upon which the order of acquittal is founded.

( 2 ) The Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 puts no limitation, restriction or condition on exercise of such power and an appellate court on the evidence before it may reach its own conclusion, both on questions of fact and of law.

(3) Various expressions, such as, "substantial and compelling reasons", "good and sufficient grounds", "very strong circumstances", "distorted conclusions", "glaring mistakes", etc. are not intended to curtail extensive powers of an appellate court in an appeal against acquittal.

Such phraseologies are more in the nature of "flourishes of language" to emphasise the reluctance of an appellate court to interfere with acquittal than to curtail the power of the court to review the evidence and to come to its own conclusion.

sentences.text: An appellate court, however, must bear in mind that in case of acquittal, there is double presumption in favour of the accused.

Firstly, the presumption of innocence is available to him under the fundamental principle of criminal jurisprudence that every person shall be presumed to be innocent unless he is proved guilty by a competent court of law.
Secondly, the accused having secured his acquittal, the presumption of his innocence is further reinforced, reaffirmed and strengthened by the trial court.

20. In the case of MUNISHAMAPPA & OTHERS v. STATEOF KARNATAKA & CONNECTED APPEALS , at paragraph 16 of the judgment it is held as under:
"16.

sentences.text: The High Court in the present case was dealing with an appeal against acquittal.
In such a case, it is well settled that the High Court will not interfere with an order of acquittal merely because it opines that a different view is possible or even preferable.
The High Court, in other words, should not interfere with an order of acquittal merely because two views are possible.
The interference of the High Court in such cases is governed by well-established principles.

According to these principles, it is only where the appreciation of evidence by the trial court is capricious or its conclusions are without evidence that the High Court may reverse an order of acquittal.

The High Court may be justified in interfering where it finds that the order of acquittal is not in accordance with law and that the approach of the trial court has led to a miscarriage of justice. ..."

In the case of HARI RAM & OTHERS v. STATE OF RAJASTHAN3, at paragraph 4 of the judgment, it is observed thus:

It is too well settled that the power of the High Court, while hearing an appeal against an acquittal is as wide and comprehensive as in an appeal against a conviction and it had full power to re- appreciate the entire evidence, but if two views on the evidence are reasonably possible, one supporting the acquittal and the other indicating conviction, then the High Court would not be justified 2000 SCC OnLine 933 - 13 - NC: 2023:KHC:45293 in interfering with the acquittal, merely because it feels that it would sitting as a trial court, have taken the other view.
While re- appreciating the evidence, the rule of prudence requires that the High Court should give proper weight and consideration to the views of the learned trial Judge.

But if the judgment of the Sessions Judge was absolutely perverse, legally erroneous and based on wrong appreciation of the evidence, then it would be just and proper for the High Court to reverse the judgment of acquittal, recorded by the Sessions Judge, as otherwise, there would be gross miscarriage of justice...."

sentences.text: The scope of interference in an appeal against acquittal is very limited.
Unless it is found that the view taken by the Court is impossible or perverse, it is not permissible to interfere with the finding of acquittal.
Equally if two views are possible, it is not permissible to set aside an order of acquittal, merely because the Appellate Court finds the way of conviction to be more probable.
The interference would be warranted only if the view taken is not possible at all."
